kurals.tamil:
அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ் ஆர்வலர்
புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbirkum undo adaikkundhaazh aarvalar,
Punkaneer poosal tharum.
kurals.meaning: Is there any bolt that can lock love up inside? The small tears that fall from a loving person's eyes when someone dear is suffering will publish that hidden love to the whole world.
kurals.elementary: Imagine trying to keep a puppy shut inside a box — it will still wiggle and whine and everyone will know it's there. Love is like that. Even if you never say "I love you," the moment someone you care about gets hurt, your eyes fill up and everybody can see exactly how you feel.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter on அன்பு (anbu, love) with an argument from evidence rather than exhortation. தாழ் (thaazh) is the wooden bolt or latch of a door, and the rhetorical question அடைக்குந்தாழ் உண்டோ — "is there a latch that shuts it in?" — treats love as a physical presence that leaks past every attempt at concealment. The proof offered is deliberately small: புன்கணீர் (punkaneer), literally "mean" or "slight" eye-water, a single involuntary tear shed for an ஆர்வலர் (aarvalar, one who is loved/desired). The commentator Parimelalhagar notes that love may not be available to காட்சி அளவை (perception) directly, yet it is established by அனுமான அளவை (inference) — a striking use of the technical vocabulary of Indian epistemology to argue that inner states are publicly readable through their effects. பூசல் (poosal) means a public outcry or uproar, so the couplet's paradox is that the quietest possible sign makes the loudest possible announcement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A devotee whose speech is sometimes choked up, whose heart melts, who cries continually and sometimes laughs, who feels ashamed and cries out loudly and then dances — a devotee thus fixed in loving service to Me purifies the entire universe.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Uddhava that genuine love for God cannot stay inside a person; it breaks out involuntarily as a choked voice, uncontrollable weeping, and even dancing.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's point: love overflows the body's locks, and tears are the first thing to escape.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 11.14.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; near-identical claim that love is betrayed by involuntary tears, though the object of love is God rather than a suffering friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!”
christianity.explanation: At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, Jesus breaks down in tears, and the bystanders immediately read those tears as evidence of how deeply he had loved the dead man.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's mechanism acted out literally: the tear is what tells the crowd about the love.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 11:35–36, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the onlookers' reaction is an almost word-for-word enactment of 'the tear proclaims the love.'

islam.quote_or_event: “The eyes are shedding tears and the heart is grieved, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord, O Ibrahim!”
islam.explanation: When his infant son Ibrahim died, the Prophet Muhammad wept; challenged by Ibn ʿAwf for weeping, he answered that this was mercy (raḥma), then spoke these words.
islam.tie_back: The Prophet does not try to latch his love away — he names the tears as the visible overflow of an inward bond.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1303 (Book of Funerals), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik
islam._accuracy_note: Wording verified against the standard sunnah.com English rendering; minor variation exists across translations of the same Arabic text.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him… And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph has spent the whole scene disguised and composed before his brothers; the love he has been suppressing finally bursts out as weeping so loud that the Egyptian court hears it.
judaism.tie_back: A textbook case of the Kural's claim — the bolt fails, and the tears become a public announcement (பூசல்).
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the narrative explicitly turns on the impossibility of holding love in.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the account of the Buddha's final days, the attendant Ānanda withdraws to a doorpost and weeps at the news that his teacher will soon pass away; the Buddha sends for him and gently acknowledges his long devotion before teaching him about impermanence.
buddhism.explanation: Ānanda tries to go off alone precisely so no one will see him cry, but his grief is discovered and read by the community as the measure of his attachment and love.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the attempt to shut love away behind a door fails, and tears betray it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested episode; the match on 'tears reveal hidden love' is strong, but the sutta's own emphasis is on non-attachment rather than on love's visibility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Odysseus concealed the tears he shed from all the rest, but Alcinous alone marked him and took heed, for he sat by him, and heard him groaning heavily.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At the Phaeacian feast, Odysseus pulls his cloak over his head to hide his weeping as the bard sings of Troy, but the king sitting beside him notices anyway.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's image exactly — a man bolts his feelings behind a cloak, and the tears still give him away.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.93–95, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified against the Perseus/Murray text; the concealment-and-detection structure matches closely, though Odysseus' tears are chiefly grief and longing rather than love for a suffering friend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.”
philosophy.explanation: Adam Smith opens his moral philosophy by arguing that fellow-feeling is not chosen or calculated but built into human nature and triggered automatically by the sight of another's condition.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith gives the Kural's claim a philosophical form: the response to another's suffering is involuntary, which is precisely why it cannot be bolted in.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part I, Section I, Chapter I
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim opening sentence; strong on involuntariness of sympathy, weaker on the specific image of tears as public testimony.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர் அன்புடையார்
என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbilaar ellaam thamakkuriyar anbudaiyaar,
Enbum uriyar pirarkku.
kurals.meaning: People without love claim everything as their own; people who have love regard even their own bones as belonging to others.
kurals.elementary: Think about two kids with a bag of sweets. One says, "These are mine, nobody touch them." The other hands them around until the bag is empty, and is happier for it. This kural says a loving person gives so completely that they would give away their very bones if it helped someone else.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a sharp antithesis of possession: எல்லாம் தமக்கு உரியர் ("all things belong to them") versus என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு ("even bones belong to others"). The word உரிமை/உரியர் is a legal term of ownership, so Valluvar is deliberately using the vocabulary of property law to describe self-giving. என்பு (enbu, bone) is the harshest, least giveable part of the body — the opposite of the money or grain one might expect a charity verse to mention — and its choice pushes generosity past the limit of comfort. Note also the chapter's internal sound-play: அன்பு (love) and என்பு (bone) are near-rhymes that Valluvar will exploit again in Kurals 73, 77 and 80, binding the ethical argument to the anatomy of the body. Many commentators, including Manakkudavar and Parimelalhagar, read the second line as covering not only the corpse but the whole living self placed at the disposal of others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sage Dadhīci, asked by the gods for a weapon that could destroy the demon Vṛtra, voluntarily gives up his own body so that his spine can be forged into the thunderbolt (vajra) that saves the worlds.
hinduism.explanation: Dadhīci's asceticism had made his bones uniquely hard, and rather than refuse, he yields his skeleton to the common good and abandons the body by yogic will.
hinduism.tie_back: This is Kural 72's second line taken absolutely literally: a loving man whose very bones belonged to others.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 6.10 — the story of Dadhīci
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Purāṇic episode (also in the Ṛg Veda and Mahābhārata); the bone imagery makes it an unusually exact parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus names self-surrender to the point of death as the definitive measure of love, spoken on the night before his own execution.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural's scale: love is measured not by what one gives away but by whether one's own body is still one's own.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:13, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; same logic of the loving person belonging to others, though framed as a single act rather than a settled disposition.

islam.quote_or_event: “They give ˹the emigrants˺ preference over themselves even though they may be in need. And whoever is saved from the selfishness of their own souls, it is they who are ˹truly˺ successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qurʾān praises the Anṣār of Medina, who housed and fed the refugees from Mecca while themselves in poverty — the virtue called īthār, preferring others over oneself.
islam.tie_back: The verse draws the same line Valluvar draws: the loveless hoard for themselves, the loving treat what is theirs as belonging to others.
islam.source: Qurʾān 59:9 (Sūrat al-Ḥashr), The Clear Quran, trans. Dr. Mustafa Khattab
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com; the contrast of īthār with shuḥḥ (soul-selfishness) maps directly onto the couplet's two halves.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self only, what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel the Elder's three-part aphorism refuses both self-neglect and self-enclosure, insisting that a life lived only for oneself forfeits its claim to be a human life at all.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel's middle clause is Valluvar's first line: the person who is only for himself has become something less than a person.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified against Sefaria's text; captures the self/other antithesis precisely, though it stops short of the Kural's 'even my bones' extremity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jātaka, the Bodhisatta born as a hare has nothing to offer a hungry traveller, so he shakes the insects from his fur and throws himself into the fire so that his own body may serve as the guest's meal.
buddhism.explanation: The tale is the canonical Buddhist illustration of dāna-pāramī, the perfection of giving, where the gift is the giver's own flesh because nothing else is available.
buddhism.tie_back: The hare's body is not his own to keep — precisely the Kural's claim that the loving hold even their bones on behalf of others.
buddhism.source: Sasa Jātaka (Jātaka no. 316), Pāli Jātaka collection
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canonical tale; the total bodily self-gift matches the couplet closely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Fates allow Admetus to escape death if someone will die in his place, his parents refuse, and only his wife Alcestis consents; she dies for him and is later brought back from the underworld by Heracles.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides' play turns on the fact that everyone in Admetus' household regards their own life as their own — except Alcestis, whose love makes hers transferable.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The play stages the Kural's two lines as two characters: the loveless keeping what is theirs, the loving surrendering even the body.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of the play's premise; the contrast between the self-keeping parents and the self-giving wife is an unusually neat parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is true of the good man too that he does many acts for the sake of his friends and his country, and if necessary dies for them; for he will throw away both wealth and honours and in general the goods that are objects of competition.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that proper self-love is not hoarding but spending — the good person secures what is truly noble by giving away the goods everyone else competes for.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle inverts ownership the way Valluvar does: the loving person's goods, and finally his life, are held on others' account.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a, trans. W. D. Ross
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; strong philosophical parallel, though Aristotle grounds it in self-love rightly understood rather than in anbu as such.

kurals.tamil:
அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கென்ப ஆருயிர்க்கு
என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbodu iyaindha vazhakkenba aaruyirkku,
Enbodu iyaindha thodarbu.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that the precious life's union with a body of flesh and bone exists for the sake of a life lived in union with love — love is the reason the soul is embodied at all.
kurals.elementary: Why do you have a body at all — arms, hands, a voice? This kural says: so that you can love people with them. A hug needs arms. Helping needs hands. The body is the tool love uses, and that is what it is for.
kurals.university: This is the philosophical hinge of the chapter. The couplet pairs two uses of இயைந்த (iyaindha, "joined with"): the soul's joining with என்பு (bone/body) and the life's joining with அன்பு (love), and asserts that the first exists as the வழக்கு — the settled practice, warrant, or rationale — of the second. ஆருயிர் (aaruyir, "rare/precious life") marks the soul as something hard-won, which sharpens the question of what it is embodied for. Parimelalhagar and later commentators read the verse causally, with some giving it a karmic gloss (embodiment as the fruit of love practised in a former birth) and others, including modern readers like M. Varadarajan, reading it teleologically: bodily existence is *for* loving. Either way Valluvar refuses a view in which the body is a mere prison for the soul — a pointed position in a South Asian intellectual landscape crowded with world-renouncing ascetic schools — and instead makes embodied relationship the point of having been born.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Teaching his wife Maitreyī before renouncing the world, Yājñavalkya explains that a husband is not dear for the husband's sake, nor a wife for the wife's sake, nor wealth or children for their own sakes — all are dear for the sake of the Self.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad grounds every particular love in a single underlying reality, making love rather than possession the thread that runs through all relationships.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats love as the reason our embodied attachments exist at all rather than as an accidental feature of them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Faithful paraphrase, but the Upaniṣad redirects love toward the Self while the Kural keeps it directed at other embodied beings — a real philosophical divergence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.”
christianity.explanation: James argues that an inward commitment which never becomes embodied action is not a live thing at all, using the body-and-spirit pair as his analogy.
christianity.tie_back: James uses exactly Valluvar's structure — the soul/body bond as the model for a virtue that must be joined to lived conduct.
christianity.source: Epistle of James 2:26, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the analogical structure matches very closely, though James's subject is faith-and-works rather than love-and-life.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of the believers in their affection, mercy, and compassion for each other is that of a body: when any limb aches, the whole body reacts with sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the community of believers as a single organism in which love is the connective tissue that makes one person's pain register in everyone else.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the bone-and-body image to say that love is what makes a collection of parts into one living thing.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6011 (also Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2586), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr
islam._accuracy_note: Wording verified against standard English renderings of the hadith; shared body imagery, though applied to the community rather than the individual soul.

judaism.quote_or_event: Commenting on “love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), Rabbi Akiva declares: “This is a great principle of the Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Akiva singles out one commandment as the organising principle from which the entire body of Jewish law takes its sense.
judaism.tie_back: Both make love the rationale that the rest of a life — or a legal system — is arranged around, not one item within it.
judaism.source: Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; cf. Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4
judaism._accuracy_note: The Akiva dictum is verified and famous; the match is thematic (love as organising principle) rather than sharing the Kural's soul-body imagery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha takes the most embodied, most instinctive human love — a mother's — and prescribes it as the model for an unrestricted attitude toward every creature.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats embodied love as the standard and purpose of a living being's existence, not as a private sentiment.
buddhism.source: Karaṇīya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.8 / Khuddakapāṭha 9, trans. Amaravati Sangha
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Amaravati translation on Access to Insight; strong on love as a whole-life orientation, weaker on the specific soul-body claim.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an aged couple who unknowingly host the disguised Zeus and Hermes, ask as their reward only that neither should outlive the other; at the end of their lives they are transformed into an oak and a linden growing from one spot, their branches intertwined.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives the pair a single fate because their lives had already become a single life; even their transformed bodies remain joined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is Valluvar's image of a life and a body inseparably joined by love, rendered as a pair of trees that cannot be separated.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate retelling; the 'inseparable union' theme fits well, but the tale is about two people rather than about soul and body.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Empedocles taught that the four roots of all things are moved by two opposing cosmic powers, Love (Philotēs) and Strife (Neikos): Love draws the elements together into living, articulated bodies, while Strife pulls them apart again.
philosophy.explanation: In his physics, love is not a feeling added onto matter but the literal binding force that assembles scattered elements into a living creature.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in cosmological form — the joining of life to flesh and bone is itself the work of love.
philosophy.source: Empedocles of Acragas, On Nature, fragments DK B17, B35 (5th century BCE)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of the surviving fragments; the parallel is genuinely structural (love as what binds body to life) though Empedocles' Love is impersonal and physical.

kurals.tamil:
அன்புஈனும் ஆர்வம் உடைமை அதுஈனும்
நண்பு என்னும் நாடாச் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbu eenum aarvam udaimai adhu eenum,
Nanbu ennum naadaach chirappu.
kurals.meaning: Love gives birth to warm eagerness toward others, and that eagerness in turn gives birth to friendship — an excellence so great that it exceeds anything one could go looking for.
kurals.elementary: Love works like a seed that grows into a plant that makes more seeds. First you care about somebody. Then you want to be around them and do things for them. Then, before you notice, you have a friend — and friendship is one of the best things anyone can have.
kurals.university: The couplet is constructed as a genealogy, with ஈனும் (eenum, "begets, gives birth to") repeated to stage a two-step generation: அன்பு → ஆர்வம் → நண்பு. ஆர்வம் (aarvam) is warm eagerness or attentive desire toward another — the same root that gave ஆர்வலர் in Kural 71 — and Valluvar places it as the middle term that converts a disposition into a relationship. The closing phrase நாடாச் சிறப்பு is the verse's most striking move: நாடா means "unsought" or "not to be searched out," so friendship is an excellence that cannot be acquired by pursuit and arrives only as the by-product of love already given. This anticipates the entire நட்பியல் (the book of friendship, chapters 79–87) in the Poruṭpāl, and it separates Valluvar from purely transactional accounts of alliance: friendship here is emergent, not negotiated.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That very ancient science of the relationship with the Supreme is today told by Me to you because you are My devotee as well as My friend.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the highest teaching is being entrusted to him not because of rank or learning but because of the affectionate friendship (sakhya) between them.
hinduism.tie_back: Devotional love is what produces the friendship, and the friendship is what makes the greatest good available — the Kural's sequence exactly.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 4.3, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; sakhya-bhakti (friendship as a mode of love) is a good match, though the Gītā does not lay out love→eagerness→friendship as stages.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus reclassifies his disciples from servants to friends, and the reclassification follows directly on his command that they love one another.
christianity.tie_back: Friendship is presented, as in the Kural, as the crowning outcome of love rather than as a separate arrangement.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:15, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; sits in the immediate context of the 'love one another' commandment, so the love→friendship progression is explicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes an outward-turning desire for another's good — not merely refraining from harm — a condition of faith itself.
islam.tie_back: This is precisely Valluvar's middle term ஆர்வம்: love turned into active eagerness for another's welfare, which is what makes people friends.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 13 (Book of Belief), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against sunnah.com; excellent match on love generating other-directed desire, slightly less explicit about friendship as the outcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
judaism.explanation: The text describes friendship arising spontaneously and involuntarily out of love — Jonathan does not decide to befriend David; the bond simply forms.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's நாடாச் சிறப்பு, the unsought excellence: friendship that is not gone looking for but is begotten by love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the spontaneity and the love→friendship causation both match the couplet unusually well.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Correcting Ānanda's guess that good friendship is half the spiritual life, the Buddha says it is the entirety of it, since the whole path unfolds from it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank friendship at the very top of the scale of goods — Valluvar's "excellence beyond seeking" and the Buddha's "whole of the holy life."
buddhism.source: Upaḍḍha Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.2, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Access to Insight translation; very strong on the supreme value of friendship, though the Buddha derives the path from friendship rather than friendship from love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pythias, condemned to death by the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, is allowed to go home to settle his affairs only because Damon offers to stand as hostage and die in his place; Pythias returns just in time, and the astonished tyrant releases them both and asks to be admitted to their friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend's whole point is that a bond of affection produced a degree of mutual trust the tyrant had assumed impossible between human beings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The tyrant's request to join them dramatises Valluvar's நாடாச் சிறப்பு — friendship as an excellence that cannot be obtained by asking for it.
greek_mythology.source: The legend of Damon and Pythias, recounted in Cicero, De Officiis III.45 and Valerius Maximus, Memorable Doings and Sayings IV.7
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Composite retelling from several ancient sources with no single canonical text; the thematic match to 'friendship as supreme unsought excellence' is strong.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle opens his two books on friendship by ranking philia above every other external good, arguing it is both a virtue and the condition of a liveable life.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle's valuation matches the Kural's: friendship is not one good among many but the excellence that makes the rest worth having.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a, trans. W. D. Ross
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; Aristotle also derives true philia from goodwill and affection, closely paralleling the couplet's sequence.

kurals.tamil:
அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கென்ப வையகத்து
இன்புற்றார் எய்தும் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbutru amarndha vazhakkenba vaiyagaththu,
Inbutraar eydhum sirappu.
kurals.meaning: The distinction enjoyed by those who live happily in this world is, the wise say, simply the fruit of a life settled in love.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever noticed that the happiest people you know are usually the ones with the most love around them — not the ones with the most stuff? This kural says that is not a coincidence. The good life people admire grows out of loving.
kurals.university: Kural 75 reuses the frame of Kural 73 — வழக்கென்ப, "the wise call it the natural practice/consequence of" — but shifts the payoff from metaphysics to lived happiness. The key verb is அமர்ந்த (amarndha), "settled, seated, at rest in": love here is not a passing rush of feeling but a stable condition one dwells in. சிறப்பு (sirappu) denotes honour, distinction, the visible excellence others recognise in a life. Crucially Valluvar locates this reward வையகத்து, "in this world," not in a heaven — a consistent feature of his ethics, which repeatedly argues that virtue pays here and now in the ordinary domestic register of the இல்லறவியல் (the book of household life). The couplet therefore functions as a rebuttal of the assumption that the loving must sacrifice their own happiness: for Valluvar, love is not the price of a good life but its mechanism.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress… such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's portrait of the devotee he holds dearest is built almost entirely from relational qualities — friendliness, compassion, absence of envy — rather than ritual or ascetic achievement.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a loving disposition the source of a person's highest standing rather than a separate obligation.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 12.13–14, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the distinction conferred is divine favour rather than worldly happiness, which is a real difference from the Kural's 'in this world'.

christianity.quote_or_event: “God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him.”
christianity.explanation: The letter identifies love not as a commandment issued by God but as the very medium in which God is present, so that to inhabit love is to inhabit God.
christianity.tie_back: The verb 'dwelleth' matches Valluvar's அமர்ந்த — love as a settled dwelling-place from which the highest good follows.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; excellent on love as an abiding state, though the promised good is union with God rather than worldly felicity.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties the mercy a person receives directly to the mercy they extend to others, making compassion the mechanism of one's own well-being.
islam.tie_back: Both texts claim the good life returns to the loving person as a consequence of the loving, not as an unrelated reward.
islam.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 1924, narrated by ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr
islam._accuracy_note: Wording verified against sunnah.com's English rendering; mercy rather than love is the operative term, and the payoff is partly otherworldly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb sets the cheapest possible meal eaten among people who love one another against a feast of fattened beef eaten in hatred, and declares the first better.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in a single domestic image: the happiness people envy in a household comes from love in it, not from what is on the table.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; an unusually close match — both are wisdom-literature couplets locating this-worldly happiness in love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One sleeps easily, wakes easily, dreams no evil dreams. One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists eleven concrete, largely present-life benefits that follow from cultivating mettā — beginning with sleeping well and being beloved by those around one.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural's claim: the ordinary, visible good fortune of a happy life is the fruit of love.
buddhism.source: Mettānisaṁsa Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.16, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the sutta is explicitly a list of this-life benefits of loving-kindness, matching வையகத்து ('in this world') precisely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord, a great grief to their foes and a joy to their friends.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, shipwrecked and in rags, blesses the princess Nausicaa with what he considers the supreme human good: a household held together by likemindedness (homophrosynē).
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus names the same prize Valluvar does — the distinction of a happy life on earth — and grounds it in loving concord at home.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.182–185, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Perseus/Murray text; strong match, and notably both sit within a 'household life' ethical frame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all the things which wisdom acquires to produce the blessedness of the complete life, far the greatest is the possession of friendship.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus, whose entire ethics is organised around a settled, untroubled happiness, ranks friendship first among everything wisdom can supply toward it.
philosophy.tie_back: Epicurus and Valluvar agree that loving bonds are not a cost to one's own happiness but the single largest contributor to it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim across standard translations; an exceptionally close philosophical parallel to the couplet's this-worldly happiness claim.

kurals.tamil:
அறத்திற்கே அன்புசார் பென்ப அறியார்
மறத்திற்கும் அஃதே துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Araththirke anbusaar benba ariyaar,
Maraththirkum aqdhe thunai.
kurals.meaning: Only the ignorant say that love is the support of virtue alone; love is just as much the support of forceful, martial action.
kurals.elementary: People think being loving means being soft. But think of a mother bird when something comes near her nest — she will fight anything. The same love that makes you gentle is what makes you brave when someone you love is in danger.
kurals.university: This is the most counter-intuitive couplet in the chapter and the one most argued over by commentators. The pair அறம் / மறம் (aram / maram) is a classical Tamil opposition: aram is righteousness and dharma, while maram is martial valour, ferocity, the warrior's fighting spirit (the word also shades toward "wrath" or "cruelty"). Valluvar's claim is that அன்பு is the துணை — the support, companion, aid — of both. Parimelalhagar reads maram narrowly, as the legitimate severity with which a ruler punishes wrongdoing; modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read it broadly as வீரம், heroism. Either way the verse blocks a sentimental reading of the whole chapter: love in the Kural is not synonymous with mildness, and Valluvar will later devote whole chapters to armies, kingship and punishment without contradiction. The underlying logic is that ferocity in defence of what one loves is itself a form of love, not its abandonment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Hanumān, searching for the captive Sītā out of devotion to Rāma, allows himself to be captured in Laṅkā and, when the demons set his tail alight, turns the humiliation into an assault that burns the city — an act of extraordinary destructive force arising wholly from love for his lord.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kāṇḍa presents Hanumān's ferocity as inseparable from his bhakti; he is gentle to Sītā in the same episode in which he devastates Rāvaṇa's capital.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly Valluvar's point — the same anbu that supports virtue also supplies the nerve for maram.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki, Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara Kāṇḍa (the burning of Laṅkā)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of a central episode; a strong illustration of love fuelling martial force, though the epic does not state the principle abstractly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables.”
christianity.explanation: The Gospels' gentlest figure acts with deliberate physical force against those exploiting worshippers; John's narrator glosses it as consuming zeal for God's house.
christianity.tie_back: The episode is the Christian counter-example to 'love is only ever mild' — the same love underwrites the whip.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 2:15, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; a well-recognised instance of love expressing itself as force, though 'zeal' rather than 'love' is the text's own term.

islam.quote_or_event: “And what is [the matter] with you that you fight not in the cause of Allah and [for] the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, 'Our Lord, take us out of this city of oppressive people…'”
islam.explanation: The verse rebukes believers for inaction and grounds the obligation to fight explicitly in compassion for the defenceless who are being oppressed.
islam.tie_back: Here the Qurʾān makes love and pity the motive for maram, which is precisely the Kural's contention.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; an unusually direct scriptural statement that compassion for the oppressed is the ground of legitimate force.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Abram hears that his nephew Lot has been carried off by a coalition of kings, he arms three hundred and eighteen trained men of his own household, pursues the raiders as far as Dan, defeats them by night and brings Lot and all the captives back.
judaism.explanation: Abram, elsewhere a peaceable herdsman who avoids quarrels, mounts a night raid purely because a kinsman he loves has been taken.
judaism.tie_back: Love of kin is what converts a peaceable man into a warrior — the Kural's claim in narrative form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Faithful paraphrase of the biblical narrative; the text does not name love as the motive explicitly, though kinship obligation is plainly the driver.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahāyāna tale of the sea-captain "Great Compassion," the Bodhisattva learns that a bandit aboard his ship plans to murder five hundred merchants; out of compassion both for the merchants and for the bandit, who would otherwise incur unimaginable karmic ruin, he kills the bandit himself and accepts the karmic consequence.
buddhism.explanation: The story is the classic Buddhist test case for whether compassion can ever require a violent act, and it answers yes — provided the motive is wholly love and the actor accepts the cost.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the nearest Buddhist analogue to the Kural's claim that love underwrites maram as well as aram.
buddhism.source: Upāyakauśalya Sūtra (Skill-in-Means Sūtra), the tale of the sea-captain
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest low rating: Buddhism's mainstream commitment is to ahiṃsā, and this is a contested Mahāyāna edge case rather than a central teaching — the best available match, not a strong one.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles has withdrawn from the Trojan war and no appeal to honour or plunder can move him; only the death of Patroclus, whom he loved, sends him back to the field, where he fights with a ferocity that terrifies gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad makes love, not martial ambition, the hinge of its plot: grief for a beloved companion produces the poem's most devastating violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Iliad is a four-hundred-page demonstration of the Kural's line that love is the ally of maram.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Books XVIII–XXII (the wrath of Achilles after Patroclus' death)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of the epic's central turn; one of the clearest illustrations in world literature of love as the engine of ferocity.

philosophy.explanation: Augustine's maxim, preached on 1 John, argues that once charity is genuinely the root of an act, the same charity may express itself as severity, rebuke or punishment just as readily as as indulgence — the outward form varies, the root does not.
philosophy.tie_back: Augustine supplies the principle behind Valluvar's couplet: love licenses sternness as well as gentleness, because both can be its instruments.
philosophy.source: Augustine of Hippo, Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Tractate VII.8 (c. 407 CE)
philosophy._accuracy_note: The Latin 'dilige et quod vis fac' and its context are verified; the traditional English rendering is quoted here, and Augustine's surrounding argument matches the Kural's logic closely.

kurals.tamil:
என்பி லதனை வெயில்போலக் காயுமே
அன்பி லதனை அறம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enbi ladhanai veyilpolak kaayume,
Anbi ladhanai aram.
kurals.meaning: Just as the blazing sun scorches the boneless creature that creeps in the open, so righteousness itself scorches the life that has no love in it.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever seen a worm caught on hot pavement in the sun? It has no shell and no bones, so it shrivels fast. This kural says a person with no love in them is just as unprotected — goodness itself will feel unbearable to them.
kurals.university: The couplet works by a tight phonetic parallel: என்பு இலதனை ("the boneless one") and அன்பு இலதனை ("the loveless one") differ by a single vowel, so the analogy is carried in the sound before the sense arrives. The traditional referent of என்பிலது is the earthworm or grub, a creature with no skeleton, which the Tamil commentators from Manakkudavar onward identify explicitly (புழு, worm). The force of the verse lies in its reversal of expectation: அறம் (aram, righteousness/dharma) is normally the protector, but here it is the destroyer — not because it attacks, but because the loveless creature has no internal structure with which to withstand it. Valluvar is claiming that love is to moral life what bone is to a body: the load-bearing frame. Without it, exposure to the moral order is simply lethal. This also sets up Kurals 79 and 80, which make the anatomical metaphor explicit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The classic formulation of dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: dharma is not a passive rule but an active power that protects those who uphold it and turns destructive toward those who do not.
hinduism.tie_back: Identical logic to the Kural — righteousness itself, not an external punisher, consumes the one who fails it.
hinduism.source: Manusmṛti (Laws of Manu) 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Bühler translation; a very close structural match, though Manu's trigger is violating dharma rather than specifically lacking love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then shall he answer them, saying, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgement scene, those condemned are not accused of any crime — only of failing to feed, clothe and visit — and their sentence is to everlasting fire.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the absence of love is itself the fatal condition, and the moral order burns those who lack it.
christianity.source: Matthew 25:45 (in context of 25:41–46), King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the fire imagery and the 'loveless by omission' charge both align closely with the couplet.

islam.quote_or_event: “So woe to those who pray — [but] who are heedless of their prayer — those who make show [of their deeds] — and withhold [simple] assistance.”
islam.explanation: Sūrat al-Māʿūn condemns not unbelievers but scrupulous worshippers whose religion has no kindness in it; withholding even the smallest neighbourly help is what draws the woe.
islam.tie_back: Religious observance without love does not shelter a person from judgement — it exposes them, which is the Kural's point exactly.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the sūra's target — piety without compassion — is precisely the loveless person that aram scorches.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven… But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings.”
judaism.explanation: Malachi's closing oracle uses one image for two opposite effects: the same burning day that reduces the wicked to stubble rises as a healing sun over the faithful.
judaism.tie_back: Malachi supplies the Kural's exact figure — righteousness as a sun that heals some and scorches others depending on what is inside them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the coincidence of 'sun' plus 'righteousness' plus 'scorching the unworthy' makes this an unusually precise image match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts, suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verse makes suffering the automatic consequence of an unwholesome inner state, following as mechanically as a cart-wheel follows the ox.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe an impersonal moral order in which the defective inner condition generates its own torment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Standard Buddharakkhita wording; the automatic-consequence structure matches, but 'impure mind' is broader than 'lovelessness' and there is no scorching imagery.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides the Erinyes hound Orestes across the world for the murder of his mother — not as agents of any court, but as the personified reaction of violated blood-kinship itself, which will not let the offender rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies represent a pre-legal moral order in which the breach of the bond of natural love automatically generates its own relentless pursuer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like aram in the Kural, the moral order here does not merely disapprove of the loveless act — it actively torments the one who committed it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of the play; the 'moral order as active tormentor' parallel is real, though the Furies punish a specific crime rather than a general absence of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IX of the Republic Socrates argues that the tyrannical man — the person whose soul is ruled entirely by appetite and who is therefore incapable of genuine friendship — is of all human beings the most wretched, and is most wretched precisely in proportion to his power.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's claim is that injustice is not chiefly harmful because of external punishment but because it disorders the soul, leaving it permanently unsatisfied and friendless.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the loveless person's punishment is not administered from outside but arises from the moral structure of the life itself.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of the Republic's argument; strong on self-inflicted moral misery, though Plato emphasises disordered appetite rather than absence of love as such.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பகத் தில்லா உயிர்வாழ்க்கை வன்பாற்கண்
வற்றல் மரந்தளிர்த் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbagath thillaa uyirvaazhkkai vanbaarkan,
Vatral marandhalirth thatru.
kurals.meaning: A life lived without love in the heart is like a dead, dried-up tree putting out green shoots in a barren desert — an appearance of flourishing with nothing real behind it.
kurals.elementary: Picture a dry stick standing in hot sand suddenly growing green leaves. It could not really happen, and if it looked like it did, something would be wrong. This kural says a life with no love in it is like that: it might look like it is going fine, but it is not really alive.
kurals.university: The comparison is doubly impossible and that is the point. வற்றல் மரம் is a tree already dried dead, and வன்பாற்கண் is the வன்புலம் or hard, waterless tract — the பாலை landscape of classical Tamil poetics, the desert region associated in akam convention with separation and deprivation. A dead tree sprouting in the desert is not merely unlikely; the couplet's force is that it is a contradiction dressed as a phenomenon. Valluvar is not saying the loveless life is unhappy — he is saying it is not life (உயிர்வாழ்க்கை) at all, only its outward semblance. The use of the tiṇai landscape vocabulary quietly imports the whole emotional register of பாலை (barrenness, loss, the unwatered heart) into an ethical argument, a characteristic Valluvar move of compressing a poetic tradition into seven words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Teaching his son Śvetaketu, Uddālaka points to a great tree: if the living essence leaves one branch, that branch withers; if it leaves a second and a third, they wither too; but when it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree withers and dies.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad uses the withering tree to show that what looks like a living structure is only alive so long as an invisible animating essence remains in it.
hinduism.tie_back: Same image, same argument: the outward form of a life persists for a while after the thing that made it alive has gone.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Faithful paraphrase of the passage; the withering-tree image matches closely, though the animating principle there is jīva/ātman rather than love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.”
christianity.explanation: In the vine discourse — which culminates in the command to love one another — Jesus says a branch severed from its source does not slowly decline but simply becomes dead wood.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's withered tree and John's withered branch make the identical point: separation from the source of love leaves only the shape of life.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:6, King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; strong image match, and the passage's own conclusion (John 15:12) is a command to love.

islam.quote_or_event: “…a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky… And the example of a bad word is like a bad tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, not having any stability.”
islam.explanation: The Qurʾān contrasts two trees — one deeply rooted and perpetually fruiting, one torn loose and unable to stand — as images of speech and the inner state behind it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts test a life by whether its tree is genuinely rooted and watered or only standing there without any source of life.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the rooted/uprooted tree parallel is strong, though the Qurʾānic subject is the good word rather than love specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah contrasts the person who trusts in mere human strength — a shrub in a salt desert — with one rooted by water, whose leaf stays green even in drought.
judaism.tie_back: Jeremiah's desert shrub and Valluvar's dry tree in the வன்பால் are very nearly the same image used to make the same judgement.
judaism.source: Jeremiah 17:6 (in context of 17:5–8), King James Version
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the desert-and-dry-plant imagery is an exceptionally close match to the couplet's பாலை setting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of colour but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practise them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada judges a display that has everything except the one quality that would make it real — colour without scent, speech without practice.
buddhism.tie_back: Both verses describe an outward flourishing that is hollow because the inward animating quality is missing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording in the Buddharakkhita translation; the 'appearance without substance' structure matches, though the missing quality is practice rather than love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus, who has rejected every lover including the nymph Echo, falls in love with his own reflection in a pool; unable to love anything outside himself, he refuses food and drink, wastes away beside the water, and is found only as a flower.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives the incapacity for outward love a literal physiological result: a beautiful young man dies of thirst beside a spring.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Narcissus is the Kural's withered tree in the barren place — abundant water and beauty all around, and no life in him at all.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate retelling; the pairing of lovelessness with withering-away makes it a strong, though mythologically rather than proverbially framed, parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that human beings are constitutively political and relational, so a person genuinely needing no one has stepped outside the human category altogether.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, denies the self-enclosed person the status of a real human life rather than merely criticising it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a, trans. Benjamin Jowett
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Jowett translation; strong on the claim that the unrelated life is not a human life, though Aristotle's term is political community rather than love.

kurals.tamil:
புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் யாக்கை
அகத்துறுப்பு அன்பி லவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Puraththurup pellaam evanseyyum yaakkai,
Agaththuruppu anbi lavarkku.
kurals.meaning: What use are all the outward limbs and organs to those who lack love, which is the body's inner organ?
kurals.elementary: A guitar can have perfect strings, shiny wood and beautiful tuning pegs — but if there's no hollow space inside it, it makes no music. This kural says love is the inside part of a person. Without it, all the outside parts don't accomplish anything.
kurals.university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a precise anatomical contrast: புறத்து உறுப்பு (external organ/limb) against அகத்து உறுப்பு (internal organ), and then makes the startling classificatory claim that அன்பு is itself an உறுப்பு — a bodily organ, not a sentiment. யாக்கை (yaakkai) is the physical frame or corporeal body. The rhetorical question எவன் செய்யும் ("what will they accomplish?") is not asking whether the limbs are pleasant but whether they can function at all, on the analogy of a body whose vital inner organ has failed. Commentators split on the referent: Parimelalhagar and Solomon Pappaiah extend it to the "external organs" of a household — its wealth, servants and property — arguing that a home without love is equally inoperative, while Varadarajan and Karunanidhi keep it to the individual body. Both readings converge on the same deflationary verdict about outward equipment, and the verse reads as a direct ancestor of the argument in Kural 80.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna distinguishes genuine discipline from its imitation: outwardly immobilised organs of action mean nothing if what is inside is unchanged.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses judge the body's outward apparatus worthless when the inner condition is absent.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 3.6, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the outward-organs/inward-state contrast matches well, though the inner quality at stake is detachment rather than love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul concedes every impressive outward performance — eloquence, prophecy, total almsgiving, martyrdom — and declares each one to be worth exactly nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: This is Valluvar's எவன் செய்யும் answered in full: the external apparatus, however complete, accomplishes nothing without the inner organ.
christianity.source: 1 Corinthians 13:3 (in context of 13:1–3), King James Version
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; one of the closest cross-tradition matches in the entire chapter — both texts even use the body as the thing rendered useless.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your bodies nor to your faces but He looks to your hearts.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, pointing to his chest as he spoke, denies that outward form or status carries any weight in divine assessment, which attends only to the inward state.
islam.tie_back: Precisely the Kural's hierarchy: the outward parts count for nothing beside the inner organ.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2564c, narrated by Abū Hurayra
islam._accuracy_note: Wording verified against sunnah.com; explicit body-versus-heart contrast makes it a very close match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
judaism.explanation: Samuel is about to anoint Jesse's tallest and most impressive son when he is stopped and told that stature and countenance are not what is being assessed.
judaism.tie_back: The verse states the Kural's principle as a rule of judgement: outward endowments are simply not the relevant organ.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; near-identical outward/inward contrast, though 'heart' is broader than anbu specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by a shaven head does an undisciplined man who utters lies become a monk. How can he who is full of desire and greed be a monk? He who wholly subdues evil deeds, both small and great, is called a monk, because he has overcome all evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada refuses to let the visible markers of the monastic life — the shaved head, the robe — count for anything without the inward transformation they are supposed to signify.
buddhism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: the outward apparatus, however correct, accomplishes nothing without the inner quality.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Wording verified against the Buddharakkhita translation; strong outward/inward contrast, though the inner quality is discipline rather than love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pygmalion carves an ivory woman more beautiful than any living one, dresses her, lays her on a couch and speaks to her — but she remains cold ivory until Venus, moved by his prayer, grants her life and her flesh grows warm under his hand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid dwells on the statue's flawless external form precisely to make the point that flawless form is not the same as a living body; something has to be given from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The statue is Valluvar's body with every outward organ and no inner one — perfectly equipped and entirely inert.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Accurate retelling; a vivid illustration of outward perfection without inward life, but the tale's own theme is desire and divine favour rather than love as an inner organ.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods … for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?”
philosophy.explanation: Opening his treatment of friendship (philia), Aristotle argues that wealth, office and power are worthless to someone with no bond of affection through which to use them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s question of what use the outer limbs are without love, Aristotle asks what use the outer goods are without friendship, and the answer in both is: none.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, ch. 1 (1155a) (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong structural parallel (what use are outward goods without inner affection), but Aristotle speaks of external goods and friendship, not bodily limbs and love as the body's inner organ.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை அஃதிலார்க்கு
என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbin vazhiyadhu uyirnilai aqdhilaarkku,
Enbudhol porththa udambu.
kurals.meaning: A body that moves along the path of love is what it means to be truly alive; for those without love, the body is nothing but bones wrapped in a covering of skin.
kurals.elementary: A house with people laughing and cooking inside is a home. The same house with nobody in it is just walls. This kural says a person without love is like that empty house — everything is still standing, but nobody is living there.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by pushing its anatomical argument to its conclusion. உயிர்நிலை (uyir-nilai) means the "state" or "seat" of life — the condition in which a body actually counts as living — and Valluvar makes that condition dependent on அன்பின் வழி, the path or way of love. The second line's என்பு தோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு is deliberately clinical: bone with skin stretched over it, the description of a cadaver or a scarecrow, and it completes the அன்பு/என்பு wordplay that has run through Kurals 72, 73 and 77. The couplet is frequently cited as the single most quoted line of the chapter and has become proverbial in Tamil. Philosophically it takes a definite position in a live ancient debate about what individuates a living being: Valluvar's answer is neither breath nor consciousness but relationship. A body that does not move along love's path may be biologically intact and is nonetheless, by his definition, not the seat of a life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Certainly that heart is steel-framed which, in spite of one's chanting the holy name of the Lord with concentration, does not change when ecstasy takes place, tears fill the eyes and the hairs stand on end.”
hinduism.explanation: The Bhāgavata diagnoses a devotee who performs every practice correctly yet feels nothing as having a heart made of metal rather than flesh.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts identify an unloving interior as a kind of non-living material — steel in one case, dry bone and skin in the other.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 2.3.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the 'unloving heart is dead matter' image matches well, though the love in question is directed at God.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.”
christianity.explanation: The letter asserts that love is not evidence of spiritual life but its actual criterion — those who do not love are described as still residing in death, present tense.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's definition in five words: without love, what looks like a living person is a body in the condition of death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; both make love the literal dividing line between life and death rather than a mere virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beware! There is a piece of flesh in the body; if it becomes good (reformed) the whole body becomes good, but if it gets spoilt the whole body gets spoilt, and that is the heart.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes the condition of one internal organ determinative of the condition of the entire body, using the same part-whole anatomy the Kural uses.
islam.tie_back: Both take the inner organ, not the frame, as the thing that decides whether the whole body amounts to anything.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 52 (Book of Belief), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr
islam._accuracy_note: Wording verified against sunnah.com; very close anatomical logic, though the hadith's concern is soundness of the heart broadly rather than love specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel's promise of restoration is described as an organ transplant: the defining change is the replacement of a heart of stone with a heart capable of feeling.
judaism.tie_back: Ezekiel and Valluvar both treat the unloving person as physically miscomposed — stone where flesh should be, bone and skin where a life should be.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim KJV; the anatomical framing of moral transformation parallels the couplet closely.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ere long, alas! this body will lie upon the earth, unheeded and lifeless, like a useless log.”
buddhism.explanation: Spoken over a monk whose diseased body had been abandoned by his fellows, the verse strips the body of every claim to significance once life has left it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada's useless log and the Kural's bone wrapped in skin are the same reduction of a body without what animates it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording in the Buddharakkhita translation; the imagery matches strikingly, though the Buddhist point is impermanence rather than lovelessness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus meets the dead as bodiless shades — 'strengthless heads' that flit and gibber, that he must feed with sacrificial blood before they can even speak, and that his arms pass straight through when he tries to embrace his own mother.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's shades retain their shape and their memories but have lost everything that made them able to hold or be held by anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's loveless body from the other direction: a human form that can no longer participate in any bond, and so is not really alive.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest moderate rating: an accurate account of Homer's underworld and an evocative parallel to 'a body that is not a life', but Homer is describing actual death, not moral lovelessness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Suppose that the eye were an animal — sight would have been its soul… when seeing is removed the eye is no longer an eye, except in name — it is no more a real eye than the eye of a statue or of a painted figure.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that the soul is the actuality or functional form of a body, so an organ that cannot perform its function is an organ in name only, however intact its matter.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle supplies the exact metaphysics of Valluvar's closing line: a body that cannot do what a body is for is bone and skin bearing the name of a person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, De Anima II.1, 412b, trans. J. A. Smith
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Smith translation; an unusually precise philosophical analogue, with Aristotle's 'eye of a statue' matching the Kural's 'bones wrapped in skin'.
